blocks.text: Proteins are linear chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. A peptide bond is an amide bond formed when the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the next, with loss of water. The long chains formed by many peptide links are polypeptide chains, and each protein has specific polypeptide chains that determine its structure and function. Proteins are organised at four structural levels.

items: Primary structure: the specific sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. This sequence decides how the protein folds into its three-dimensional shape, and so its function; even one changed amino acid can impair the protein. Proteins such as albumin and insulin depend on precise sequences. In sickle-cell anaemia an abnormal haemoglobin makes red blood cells sickle-shaped; the sickle cells clog blood vessels and disturb circulation.

Secondary structure: the backbone atoms form hydrogen bonds (between C=O and N-H groups) within or between chains, giving regular patterns. In an alpha-helix the hydrogen bonds form along a single chain, giving a coiled spiral (e.g. keratin); in a beta-pleated sheet they form between neighbouring strands, giving a folded sheet (e.g. silk fibroin).

Tertiary structure: the overall three-dimensional shape formed when a chain folds because of interactions between side chains (R groups): hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions and disulphide bridges. This shape decides the function; in enzymes, the exact shape of the active site allows the substrate to bind.
Quaternary structure: in some proteins two or more folded chains (subunits) associate through hydrogen bonds, ionic (salt) bridges, hydrophobic interactions and sometimes disulphide bonds.

blocks.alt: Top: the condensation of two amino acids to a dipeptide with a -CO-NH- link and water. Below, four panels: primary, a string of coloured beads (the amino acid sequence); secondary, an alpha-helix (keratin) and a beta-pleated sheet (silk) held by hydrogen bonds; tertiary, a folded chain held by hydrogen and ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions and S-S bridges; quaternary, four folded subunits together, e.g. haemoglobin.
blocks.caption: The peptide bond and the four levels of protein structure (original diagram after Figures 27.4 to 27.6).
blocks.long_description: Each level builds on the one before. The sequence of amino acids (primary) decides which helices and sheets form (secondary), these fold into one compact shape (tertiary), and some proteins combine several folded chains (quaternary).

blocks.text: By overall shape, proteins are divided into two classes:

items: Fibrous proteins: long, rod-like or thread-like molecules whose chains run parallel and are linked by strong hydrogen bonds or disulphide bonds into fibres. They are generally insoluble in water, mechanically strong and stable, and act as structural polymers, e.g. collagen (connective tissue), keratin (hair, nails, skin) and myosin (muscle). Keratin of hair and the fibroin of silk are the fibrous proteins named in the learning outcomes.

Globular proteins: the whole molecule is spherical or oval. Most 'worker' (functional) proteins, such as enzymes, hormones and nutrient proteins, are globular. They are more sensitive to heat and pH: egg white hardens on heating because the hydrogen bonds between chains are broken and the chains open up, and the milk protein casein coagulates when lemon juice lowers the pH. This is denaturation of proteins.

blocks.prompt: What holds an alpha-helix in shape?
blocks.explanation: Hydrogen bonds between the C=O of one peptide link and the N-H of another peptide link a few amino acids further along the same chain.

items: Secondary: alpha-helix and beta-sheet (hydrogen bonds); tertiary: folding by R-group interactions; quaternary: several chains.
Fibrous (collagen, keratin) and globular (enzymes, hormones); denaturation by heat or pH.
